items.text: Welcome to Section 0: DevOps Foundation. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
0.1 What is DevOps, SRE, and Platform Engineering?

DevOps is a cultural philosophy, set of practices, and tools that increases an organization's ability to deliver applications and services at high velocity. It breaks down the traditional silos between Software Development (Dev) and IT Operations (Ops).

Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) is a discipline pioneered by Google that applies software engineering principles to operations and infrastructure challenges. SRE is 'what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team.'

Platform Engineering is the practice of designing and building toolchains and workflows that enable self-service capabilities for software engineering organizations in the cloud era. Platform engineers create an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) to establish a 'Golden Path' for developers, reducing cognitive load.
Comparing Devops, SRE, and Platform Engineering
0.2 Infrastructure Evolution: Traditional vs Cloud-Native

Infrastructure has shifted from Bare Metal (where server provisioning took weeks) to Virtual Machines (where virtualization enabled hypervisors to divide physical servers in minutes), and finally to Cloud-Native Containerization (where application environments are packaged and run in isolated user-space processes on a shared kernel in seconds).
CI/CD Culture & GitOps

GitOps is an operational framework that takes DevOps best practices used for application development, such as version control, collaboration, compliance, and CI/CD, and applies them to infrastructure automation. The Git repository is the single source of truth for the desired state of your infrastructure.
0.3 Career and Salary Roadmap

DevOps and SRE are among the highest-paying domains in tech. A career progression typically moves from Linux System Admin ($70k-$90k) -> DevOps/Cloud Engineer ($110k-$150k) -> Senior DevOps/SRE ($160k-$220k) -> Principal Infrastructure Architect / Platform Lead ($250k+).
Summary

DevOps bridges cultural gaps using automation; SRE applies software engineering to reliability; Platform Engineering creates self-service Internal Developer Platforms. GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth for desired state.
Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the difference between DevOps and SRE.
items.answer: DevOps is a set of cultural principles and practices aimed at breaking down silos between developers and operations. SRE is a concrete implementation of DevOps. SRE focuses heavily on reliability metrics (SLIs, SLOs, Error Budgets), monitoring, incident response, and automation of operational tasks using software engineering practices.

items.question: What is GitOps and how does it differ from traditional CI/CD?
items.answer: Traditional CI/CD uses pipelines that push built code or infrastructure changes to targets (e.g. running 'terraform apply' or 'kubectl apply' directly from a runner). GitOps is pull-based: a Git repository stores the declaration of the desired state, and a controller (like ArgoCD) running inside the target cluster continuously compares the desired state with the live state and pulls updates to resolve drift.

items.text: Practical Assignment

Write a comparison chart mapping your current organization's software delivery workflow against the DevOps principles. Identify two manual bottle-necks (e.g., manual ticket creation, lack of automated staging tests) and draft a 3-step action plan to automate them.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: Case Study: Silicon Valley Fintech Deployments
items.text: A financial platform experienced 30-minute deployment outages due to manual server patching and database configuration drift. By shifting to GitOps with ArgoCD and standardizing environments using Docker containers, they reduced deploy times to under 3 minutes with zero downtime, using rolling deployments and automated rollbacks on target metric anomalies.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Check if Git repo state matches the target environment.
Inspect deployment pipelines for configuration drift.
Verify that all service dependencies are documented in the deployment manifest.

items.question: How do you find which process is listening on port 80?

Welcome to Section 2: Virtual Machines & Bare Metal. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
2.1 Virtualization & Hypervisors
Virtualization allows multiple independent operating systems (VMs) to run on a single physical host by abstracting hardware resources.
• **Type 1 Hypervisors (Bare Metal)**: Run directly on host hardware (e.g. VMware ESXi, Proxmox VE, KVM). High performance, enterprise-grade.
• **Type 2 Hypervisors (Hosted)**: Run on top of an existing Operating System (e.g. VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). Ideal for local development.
Hypervisors Architecture Visualized
2.2 KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine)
KVM turns the Linux kernel into a Type-1 hypervisor. It utilizes hardware virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x or AMD-V). Operations use 'virsh' CLI to manage VMs:

lines: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-system libvirt-clients bridge-utils virtinst virt-manager
# Create a KVM Virtual Machine via CLI

items.text: Summary
Type-1 Hypervisors provide high performance by running directly on hardware. KVM integrates virtual machine management directly into the Linux kernel, using QEMU to emulate devices.
Interview Questions

items.question: What is the difference between full virtualization and paravirtualization?
items.answer: Full virtualization emulates the entire hardware, allowing unmodified Guest OSs to run. Paravirtualization modifies the Guest OS kernel to communicate directly with the hypervisor via hypercalls, improving network and disk performance significantly.

items.text: Practical Assignment
Install KVM on a local Linux server or virtual machine, configure a bridged network interface, and install an Alpine Linux instance inside a VM.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: VM Disk Exhaustion
items.text: A database VM hosted on Proxmox ran out of storage space. The SRE team resolved this by increasing the disk allocation on the host via LVM/QEMU, rescanning the SCSI bus inside the VM, resizing the physical volume, and expanding the ext4 file system inline without shutting down the VM.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Verify CPU hardware virtualization support: egrep -c '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo.
Check libvirtd service status: systemctl status libvirtd.
Verify virtual network bridges: ip link show.

Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy.
items.answer: A forward proxy hides the identity of the client (used by clients to access resources, e.g. a VPN). A reverse proxy hides the identity of the backend server (used by servers to handle client traffic, routing, SSL termination, and load balancing).

items.question: What is the use of 'proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade' in NGINX?
items.answer: This is used for WebSockets protocol upgrading. When a client requests a WebSocket connection, NGINX passes the upgrade headers to the backend node server so that the persistent connection can be successfully established.

items.text: A SaaS product experienced a Denial of Service attack where a single IP flooded the application with 500 requests per second. The SRE team quickly updated the NGINX configuration, applying limit_req_zone to throttle requests to 15 per second, returning a 429 Too Many Requests status code for abusers.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Verify NGINX configuration syntax: nginx -t.
Check systemd logs: journalctl -u node-app -f.
Verify port binding: ss -tulpn | grep nginx.
Welcome to Section 4: SSL/TLS & Certificate Management. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
4.1 SSL/TLS Handshake & PKI
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) secures communications on the web. During a TLS 1.3 handshake:
1. Client Hello: Client sends supported cipher suites and key share.
2. Server Hello: Server selects cipher, provides key share, and sends its SSL Certificate.
3. Certificate Verification: Client verifies certificate against trusted root Certificate Authorities (CAs).
4. Session Keys: Both parties generate symmetric session keys for encrypted communication.
4.2 Let's Encrypt Automation with Certbot
Let's Encrypt uses the ACME protocol to issue certificates. Standard verification is completed via HTTP-01 or DNS-01 challenges.

lines: # Install Certbot on Ubuntu for NGINX
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y certbot python3-certbot-nginx
# Obtain SSL certificate automatically configuration NGINX

items.text: Summary
TLS handshakes secure internet data. Certbot automates certificate requests and renewal from Let's Encrypt, preventing certificate expiration incidents.
Interview Questions

items.question: What is the difference between an HTTP-01 and DNS-01 certbot challenge?
items.answer: HTTP-01 requires placing a specific file at a path on the web server (port 80 must be open to the internet). DNS-01 requires creating a specific TXT DNS record, which is ideal for wildcard certificates or internal environments where port 80 is blocked.

items.title: Expired Certificates Incident
items.text: An ecommerce store went offline with security warning page blockages because the SSL certificate expired. The SRE team fixed this by resolving a port 80 redirect issue preventing ACME validation, renewing the cert inline, and configuring a script to monitor certificate expiry and alert Slack 14 days in advance.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Verify that port 80 is open to let ACME HTTP-01 validation reach the host.
Check certificate expiration using openssl x509 CLI.
Confirm that the certificate chain is complete (use fullchain.pem, not cert.pem).
Welcome to Section 5: Cloud Computing Fundamentals. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
5.1 Cloud Models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and FaaS
Cloud architectures divide operational responsibility between the customer and provider:
• **Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)**: Raw compute (VMs), storage, and networking (e.g. AWS EC2, GCP Compute Engine). You manage OS and stack.
• **Platform as a Service (PaaS)**: Managed application runtimes (e.g. Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk). You deploy code, provider manages OS.
• **Serverless / Function as a Service (FaaS)**: Event-driven execution (e.g. AWS Lambda, GCP Cloud Run). Code scales on demand, down to zero.
Cloud Service Comparison
Summary
Cloud services run from bare infrastructure (IaaS) to fully managed platforms (PaaS/FaaS). Choosing the right service involves balancing cost, setup complexity, and scaling flexibility.
Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the concept of 'shared responsibility model' in cloud computing.
items.answer: The cloud provider is responsible for securing the physical servers, virtualization hypervisors, and global network. The customer is responsible for patching guest OS, configuring firewalls (Security Groups), protecting data, and managing access IAM credentials.

items.text: Practical Assignment
Draft a cost-comparison model for hosting a web application requiring 4 cores, 8GB RAM, and 100GB persistent storage across AWS, GCP, and DigitalOcean.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: Cloud Cost Overrun
items.text: A startup was billed $25,000 in a month due to runaway dev VMs and unattached disk volumes. SRE instituted cost optimization policies: enforcing AWS budget alarms, automating the deletion of untagged resources, and scheduling dev workloads to shut down on weekends.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Verify resource quotas in the target cloud zone before provisioning.
Ensure multi-factor authentication (MFA) is active on the root account.
Configure budget alerts at 50%, 75%, and 90% of expected cloud spend.
Welcome to Section 6: Auto Scaling Groups & Managed Infrastructure. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
6.1 High Availability & Disaster Recovery

High availability (HA) ensures systems remain operational even when hardware or network components fail. We achieve HA through redundancy: hosting servers across multiple independent **Availability Zones (AZs)**.
Auto Scaling Groups & Load Balancers

An **Auto Scaling Group (ASG)** automatically launches or terminates virtual machines based on metrics like CPU utilization or network traffic. A **Load Balancer** sits in front of the ASG, distributing requests evenly across healthy virtual machine instances.
6.2 Disaster Recovery Strategies

rows: Medium (DB is hot, compute is off)

items.text: Summary
Auto Scaling handles request fluctuations. Dynamic load balancers isolate applications from single-point-of-failure instances across multiple Availability Zones.
Interview Questions

items.question: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
items.answer: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable duration of system downtime after an outage. Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable age of data loss, measuring the time between the last backup/replication and the outage.

items.text: Practical Assignment
Design a multi-AZ VPC layout using dry-erase board or design tools, showing public subnets for load balancers and private subnets for app servers and databases.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: Black Friday traffic spike
items.text: During a flash sale, traffic surged by 800% in 2 minutes. The SRE team configured the ASG with a step scaling policy based on CPU utilization and request count per target, scaling the fleet from 3 to 45 servers seamlessly without dropping checkout requests.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Verify that target group health checks are configured correctly.
Check cooldown periods on Auto Scaling scaling policies.
Confirm instance limits within the cloud provider region.
Welcome to Section 7: Containers & Container Runtimes. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
7.1 Containerization Under the Hood
Containers are not virtual machines. They are isolated processes running on the host system sharing the host's operating system kernel. Isolation is achieved via Linux kernel primitives:
• **Namespaces**: Restrict what the container can see (PID isolation, Network interface isolation, Mount isolation, IPC, UTS, User).
• **Cgroups (Control Groups)**: Restrict what resources the container can use (CPU limits, Memory limits, Disk I/O throttling).
• **Pivot Root / chroot**: Changes the root filesystem directory for the container process.
Visual Architecture Comparison: VM vs Container
7.2 OCI Standards & Container Runtimes
The Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines specifications for container runtimes and image formats:
• **Low-level runtime (runC)**: Interacts directly with the kernel to set up namespaces, cgroups, and execute container processes.
• **High-level runtime (containerd / CRI-O)**: Manages image downloads, image unpacking, container network setup, and calls runC.
Summary
Containers isolate processes on a shared kernel using namespaces and cgroups. High-level runtimes like containerd supervise these lifecycles, conforming to OCI standards.
Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the difference between PID and NET namespaces in Linux.
items.answer: The PID namespace isolates the process ID space, meaning a process inside a container cannot see or kill processes running on the host or other containers. The NET namespace isolates network devices, ports, routing tables, and firewall rules, giving each container its own virtual loopback and IP address.

items.question: What happens if a container process exceeds its memory limit configured in cgroups?
items.answer: The Linux kernel's Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer will trigger, sending a SIGKILL signal directly to the container process. The container terminates with exit code 137 (OOMKilled).

items.text: Practical Assignment
Use command line tools to inspect running namespaces on a Linux machine using 'lsns' and check container resource configuration under '/sys/fs/cgroup/'.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: Container Escape Vulnerability
items.text: A security audit flagged containers running as privileged users. SRE mitigated container breakout risks by changing all Docker images to run as non-root users, disabling privilege escalation, and utilizing namespaces for user remapping.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Inspect kernel namespaces using the 'lsns' command.
Verify cgroup configurations under '/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/'.
Check system logs for OOM events using 'dmesg -T | grep -i oom'.
Welcome to Section 8: Docker Complete Mastery. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
8.1 Multi-Stage Dockerfile Optimization

Multi-stage builds allow developers to write clean, small production container images. Heavy dependencies, compilers, and development tools are separated into a 'builder' stage, leaving only compiled assets in the final container layer.
Production Multi-Stage Dockerfile
Here is an optimized, non-root, multi-stage Dockerfile for a production Node.js application:

codeMap.dockerfile:
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
RUN npm prune --production

FROM node:18-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S nodeapp && adduser -u 1001 -S nodeapp -G nodeapp
USER nodeapp
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
EXPOSE 3001
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

items.text: 8.2 Orchestrating with Docker Compose
Deploy a multi-container stack containing a web application, a PostgreSQL database, and a Redis cache using Docker Compose:

codeMap.docker_compose:
version: '3.8'
services:
  web_app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "3001:3001"
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://admin:supersecret@db:5432/production_db
      - REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379
    depends_on:
      - db
      - cache
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_USER=admin
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=supersecret
      - POSTGRES_DB=production_db
    volumes:
      - pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
volumes:
  pg_data:

items.text: Summary
Optimized Dockerfiles use multi-stage builds and run as non-root users. Docker Compose orchestrates multi-container runtimes on developer machines or single-node VPS environments.
Interview Questions

items.question: What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?
items.answer: COPY simply copies files from the local build context into the container image. ADD has additional features: it can download files from URLs and automatically extract archive contents (tar.gz, zip) into the destination directory. COPY is preferred for its simplicity.

items.question: How does Docker caching work during image build?
items.answer: Docker processes Dockerfile instructions from top to bottom. For each line, Docker checks its cache for an existing layer. If a command or copied file changes (e.g. package.json), the cache for that layer and all subsequent layers is invalidated, requiring full execution.

items.text: Practical Assignment
Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a React application served by NGINX. Optimize the final image size to be under 30MB.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: Huge Image Deployments
items.text: A company was deploying 1.5GB Docker images, causing slow startup times and high registry costs. The platform team reorganized the Dockerfiles into multi-stage structures, reducing the final image size to 68MB and cutting deployment times from 8 minutes to 15 seconds.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Inspect Docker build history using 'docker history <image_id>'.
Check running container logs: 'docker logs -f <container_name>'.
Inspect container networks: 'docker network inspect <network_name>'.
Welcome to Section 9: Kubernetes Complete Guide (Part 1). This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
9.1 Kubernetes Architecture
Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform for automating application deployment, scaling, and management.
• **Control Plane**: Manages the cluster state. Contains 'kube-apiserver', 'etcd' (data store), 'kube-scheduler' (assigns nodes), and 'kube-controller-manager' (monitors state).
• **Worker Nodes**: Execute workloads. Contains 'kubelet' (agent managing container lifecycle), 'kube-proxy' (network rules), and container runtimes.
Kubernetes Cluster Architecture Diagram
9.2 Core Kubernetes Manifests (YAML)
Deploy a scalable application using Deployment and Service resources:

codeMap.k8s:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: lms-app-deployment
  labels:
    app: lms
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: lms
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: lms
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: lms-web
        image: node:18-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3001
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: lms-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: lms
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3001

items.text: Summary
The Control Plane coordinates the cluster; Worker Nodes execute the pods. Yaml manifests declare the desired state, which Kubernetes actively maintains.
Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the difference between a Pod and a Container.
items.answer: A container is a single executable process isolated at the OS level. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, wrapping one or more containers that share the same network namespace, storage volumes, and IP address.

items.question: What is the role of etcd in Kubernetes?
items.answer: etcd is a highly-available, distributed key-value store used to hold all cluster state data and configuration. It is the single source of truth for Kubernetes, and only the kube-apiserver communicates directly with it.

items.text: Practical Assignment
Install Minikube locally, deploy the LMS app manifest, scale the replica count to 5 using kubectl CLI, and view container status.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: Node Failure Self-Healing
items.text: A physical server in a Kubernetes cluster crashed. Within 40 seconds, the Control Plane noticed the Node status was NotReady, marked the scheduled pods as dead, and redeployed the web replicas onto healthy worker nodes automatically.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Inspect pod statuses: 'kubectl get pods -A'.
Check event logs: 'kubectl describe pod <pod_name>'.
Stream container output: 'kubectl logs <pod_name>'.
Welcome to Section 10: Kubernetes Advanced (Part 2). This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
10.1 StatefulSets & DaemonSets
• **StatefulSets**: Manage stateful applications requiring persistent storage and stable network identifiers (e.g. databases, Redis clusters). Pods are named sequentially: db-0, db-1.
• **DaemonSets**: Ensure that all (or some) nodes run a copy of a Pod (e.g. Prometheus node-exporters, Fluentd logging agents).
10.2 Ingress Routing & Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)
An **Ingress** routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to Services inside the cluster using rules. The **HPA** dynamically scales pod count up or down based on CPU/Memory metrics:

codeMap.k8s:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: main-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: learnxchain.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: lms-service
            port:
              number: 80
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: lms-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: lms-app-deployment
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 75

items.text: Summary
StatefulSets handle stateful apps; Ingress controllers route external traffic into internal services. HPAs automatically manage pod replica scaling based on real-time resource loads.
Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet.
items.answer: Deployments manage stateless pods with random suffixes; pods can be deleted or replaced at any time. StatefulSets manage pods with persistent, ordinal indexes (0, 1, 2) that mount specific persistent volumes, maintaining identity during updates.

items.question: How does HPA fetch metrics to perform scaling decisions?
items.answer: HPA queries the Kubernetes metrics-server API to retrieve CPU/Memory usage logs of pods matching target selector labels, making scaling calculations every 15 seconds.

items.text: Practical Assignment
Write a Helm chart packaging the LMS application, defining values.yaml parameters for replica count and image tags.
Real Production Scenario

items.title: Database Corruption Prevention
items.text: A database running on Kubernetes collapsed under high disk load. Because the SRE team used a StatefulSet with a persistent volume claim (PVC) template, the database pod was rescheduled onto a healthy host node, mounting the same block volume and recovering transaction logs without data loss.
Troubleshooting Checklist
Verify metrics-server installation: 'kubectl top nodes'.
Inspect Ingress rules: 'kubectl describe ingress <name>'.
Check volume attachments: 'kubectl get pv,pvc'.
Welcome to Section 11: CI/CD Complete Guide. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
11.1 CI/CD Pipelines & GitOps
Continuous Integration (CI) automates code builds, linting, and testing on commit. Continuous Deployment (CD) automates deployments into environments.
Production GitHub Actions Workflow
This workflow triggers on commits to main, installs dependencies, runs tests, builds a Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub, and triggers an deployment:

codeMap.github:
name: Production CI/CD Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
jobs:
  test-and-lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: 18
          cache: 'npm'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Run ESLint
        run: npm run lint
      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm run test
  build-and-push:
    needs: test-and-lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Set up QEMU
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v2
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}
      - name: Build and Push Image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: myorg/lms-app:${{ github.sha }},myorg/lms-app:latest

items.text: 11.2 GitOps Git Reconciliation (ArgoCD)
ArgoCD runs inside Kubernetes and syncs clusters to desired state defined in a Git repository:
Summary
CI/CD automation pipelines test and build application packages. GitOps tools like ArgoCD continuously reconcile cluster configurations with Git declarations.
Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment.
items.answer: Continuous Delivery automatically builds, tests, and prepares artifacts for deployment, requiring manual approval to push to production. Continuous Deployment automates the entire process, pushing commits directly to production automatically.

items.question: What is the 'pull' model in GitOps, and why is it preferred over 'push'?
items.answer: In the pull model, an agent in the cluster pulls updates from Git, meaning the cluster doesn't expose external credentials or API endpoints to CI runners, significantly improving security and preventing config drift.

items.text: Practical Assignment

items.title: Malicious Pipeline Access
items.text: A developer's credentials were stolen, allowing attackers to access CI tools. Because the organization used pull-based ArgoCD GitOps, the attackers could not gain write access to the Kubernetes control plane directly, containing the breach.

Check ArgoCD sync statuses: 'argocd app get <app_name>'.
Inspect CI runner execution output logs.

12.1 The Three Pillars of Observability
• **Metrics**: Numeric aggregations (CPU, RAM, Request Rate) ideal for detecting anomalies and scaling (Prometheus).
• **Logs**: Structured textual output (JSON) describing specific application events (Loki, ELK Stack).
• **Traces**: End-to-end request flows across distributed systems, showing latency bottlenecks (Jaeger, OpenTelemetry).
Prometheus Monitoring Architecture Diagram
12.2 Prometheus Configuration
Prometheus collects metrics by pulling endpoints periodically. Example 'prometheus.yml':

codeMap.yaml:
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'prometheus'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']
  - job_name: 'lms-app'
    metrics_path: '/metrics'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['lms-service.default.svc.cluster.local:3001']

items.text: Summary
Observability combines metrics, logs, and traces. Prometheus uses a pull model to collect system metrics, visualizing data in Grafana.
Interview Questions

items.question: What is the difference between Observability and Monitoring?
items.answer: Monitoring tells you WHEN a system is broken (using alerts for cpu, up status). Observability provides the internal state context to let you understand WHY it is broken (using trace paths and contextual logs).

Troubleshooting Checklist

items.question: How do you prevent state lock file issues in team setups?

Welcome to Section 15: Sandboxing & Firecracker. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
15.1 Secure Multi-Tenant Sandboxing
In multi-tenant environments (e.g., Replit, AWS Lambda, serverless runtimes), executing untrusted code requires strict isolation. Standard containers are insecure because they share the host kernel.

• **Firecracker**: An open-source virtualization technology built by AWS. It launches lightweight virtual machines (MicroVMs) using KVM in milliseconds, providing VM-level security isolation with container-level startup speeds.
15.2 Firecracker Architecture
Host OS -> Linux KVM -> Firecracker (VMM) -> MicroVM (isolated Guest kernel & rootfs).
Interacting with Firecracker API
Firecracker is controlled via a local Unix socket API. Set up a MicroVM network using curl:

items.text: Summary
Firecracker creates secure MicroVMs for serverless runtimes. It operates using local API sockets to launch isolated guest kernels in milliseconds.
Interview Questions

items.question: Why are standard containers considered less secure than microVMs for untrusted code?
items.answer: Standard containers share the same Linux kernel as the host OS. A kernel vulnerability (like a system call bug) could allow an attacker to escape the container. MicroVMs run their own guest kernels, isolating memory and syscall interfaces.

Troubleshooting Checklist

Check ownership of the Unix socket path '/tmp/firecracker.socket'.
Verify CPU configuration settings in the API payload.

items.question: Explain Cache Penetration and how to prevent it.
items.answer: Cache penetration occurs when requests repeatedly query data that does not exist, missing the cache and hitting the database. Prevent this by caching null results with short expirations or using Bloom filters.

17.1 High Availability Databases
Database engines must operate under high availability topologies to ensure uptime.
• **PostgreSQL Replication**: Achieved via streaming WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records from a Primary (Read/Write) server to Standby (Read-Only) replicas.
• **MongoDB Replica Sets**: Group of mongod processes maintaining the same data set, electing a new Primary automatically if the current one goes offline.

Interview Questions

items.question: Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous database replication.
items.answer: Synchronous replication waits for transaction verification from standby nodes before reporting success to the client, guaranteeing data safety at the cost of latency. Asynchronous replication writes to the primary and returns immediately, updating standby nodes in the background.

items.question: Explain the difference between an IAM User and an IAM Role.

Welcome to Section 24: Site Reliability Engineering. This section covers key infrastructure, automation, SRE best practices, and hands-on operational challenges.
24.1 Service Level Terminology
• **SLI (Service Level Indicator)**: A quantitative measure of a service's performance (e.g. latency of successful requests < 100ms).
• **SLO (Service Level Objective)**: A target reliability metric defined for the SLI (e.g. 99.9% of requests < 100ms over 30 days).
• **SLA (Service Level Agreement)**: The legal agreement with customers, specifying penalties if the SLO is not met.
Error Budgets

The Error Budget is the allowed downtime of a service (100% - SLO). For a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, the allowed downtime is **43.2 minutes**. When the error budget is exhausted, deployments are blocked, and engineers shift focus to reliability improvements.
24.2 SRE SLO Targets Table
Summary
SRE balances velocity with reliability using error budgets. SLOs define availability targets, and breach events trigger deployment freezes.
Interview Questions

items.question: How do you calculate an Error Budget?
items.answer: Error Budget is calculated as '1 - SLO'. For instance, if your availability SLO is 99.9%, your error budget is 0.1%. If your service serves 1,000,000 requests, you can afford to fail 1,000 requests before exhausting the budget.

items.question: What is MTTR and MTBF?
items.answer: MTTR (Mean Time to Repair) is the average time taken to restore a service after an outage. MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average operational time of a system between occurrences of failures.

items.question: What is a container image?
items.answer: A container image is a lightweight, standalone, executable package of software that includes everything needed to run an application: code, runtime, system tools, system libraries, and settings.

items.question: Explain the difference between a stateful and stateless application.
items.answer: A stateless application does not store data locally; requests can be routed to any instance (e.g. web server). A stateful application relies on local storage or database states, requiring stable network and storage identities.

items.text: Senior & Staff-level Questions

items.question: How would you design a zero-downtime database migration?
items.answer: A zero-downtime database migration involves: 1. Deploying a schema update that is backward-compatible (adding columns, not deleting). 2. Double-writing data to both old and new columns. 3. Backfilling historical data. 4. Updating code to read from the new schema. 5. Deleting old schema columns.

items.question: Explain the Kubernetes scheduling lifecycle.
items.answer: When a Pod is created, it enters the 'Pending' state. The scheduler filters nodes based on resource requests, taints/tolerations, and affinity rules. It then scores the remaining healthy nodes and binds the Pod to the node with the highest score.

items.text: 28.2 CrashLoopBackOff Diagnostics

Interview Questions

items.question: What does exit code 137 mean in a Docker container?
items.answer: Exit code 137 indicates that the container was terminated by the operating system kernel sending a SIGKILL signal. This is typically caused by the OOM (Out-Of-Memory) killer when the process exceeds its configured memory limits.

items.title: Silent DNS Failure Outage
items.text: An API server could not resolve database hostnames, failing checkout requests. The SRE team diagnosed this by checking resolv.conf, finding a misconfigured internal DNS server, and routing DNS traffic to 1.1.1.1 temporarily.
